choices: You're out, the stop did its job
Hold it, give it until the close
Buy more, it's cheaper now
Drop the stop under the week's low
questions.answer: You're out, the stop did its job
questions.why: You're out. It lost VWAP and broke the low of the day, and that's exactly what says the turn failed. A new low means the selling wasn't done. Your stop is a real order with the broker, so it already sold you. That's the point of having it there. Don't buy it back out of frustration. If it builds a new low, turns and reclaims VWAP again, that's a new trade with its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: Lose VWAP and the low, and the turn failed. The stop says so first.

wrong.Hold it, give it until the close: The stop doesn't wait for the close. By then the loss can be a lot bigger.
wrong.Buy more, it's cheaper now: Never add to a loser. Cheaper is just a bigger loss on the same broken idea.
wrong.Drop the stop under the week's low: A stop only moves up. Moving it down turns a planned loss into an open-ended one.

questions.simple: You're out. The low broke, so the turn failed, and the stop already did the work.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)
fixed before: the story said only 'a new low', which may not reach a stop a few cents under the old low

questions.q: You were a few minutes late. The trigger was 20.00 and it's trading 21.00 now. What's the play?
choices: Let it go, it's 5% past the trigger
Buy it, 5% is just momentum
Buy half size to cut the risk
Pass, any price over 20.00 chases
questions.answer: Let it go, it's 5% past the trigger
questions.why: Let it go. 21.00 minus 20.00 is 1.00, and 1.00 over 20.00 is 5%. We don't buy more than 4% past the trigger. Chasing doesn't move your stop. It's still under the low of the day. So the distance to the stop grows, your share count shrinks, and the 9 EMA target is closer than it was. Same risk, less reward. If you missed it, you missed it. There's always another setup.
questions.lesson_line: Past 4% over the trigger, let it go.

wrong.Buy it, 5% is just momentum: It's momentum you missed. Past 4% the size shrinks and so does the room to the target.
wrong.Buy half size to cut the risk: Half of a chase is still a chase. We skip it, we don't shrink it.
wrong.Pass, any price over 20.00 chases: A little over the trigger is fine. The line is 4% past it, not one cent past it.

questions.simple: Let it go. It's 5% past the trigger, and we don't chase more than 4%.

deeper.example: The stop is the day's low and it does not move. At 20.00 the distance to the stop is already set. At 21.00 that distance is larger, so the same risk buys fewer shares, and the trade has less room before the target. The chase line stops that drift at 4%.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)
computed key (5% from the calc)

questions.q: The 50-day is 180.00, ATR 4.00, the close before the climax day 150.00. How many ATR under the 50-day is it?
questions.why: 7.5 ATR. Take the 50-day minus the close, then divide by the ATR: (180.00 minus 150.00) divided by 4.00 is 7.5. Our card lists this stretch for each example, such as BABA at 6.7 ATR under its 50-day. It shows how far price ran in terms of its own normal range.
questions.lesson_line: Stretch is measured in ATRs under the 50-day. Do the division.
questions.simple: Subtract the close from the 50-day, then divide by the ATR, and you get 7.5 ATR.

reasons: computed key
the ATR cut-offs are a held decision (D-118); this item only computes the stretch

choices: 30.0 ATR
0.1 ATR
7.5 ATR

wrong.30.0 ATR: Gave the gap in dollars, no divide.
wrong.120.0 ATR: Multiplied by the ATR instead of dividing.
wrong.0.1 ATR: Flipped it: divided the ATR by the gap.

questions.q: A parabolic long only lasts a few days, so you can keep the stop in your head instead of with the broker.
questions.why: False. Every position gets a real stop order with the broker, however short the trade. A stop in your head is a debate. When price is diving through your level in a panic, you'll talk yourself into one more minute. This setup moves fast both ways, and it punishes anyone who doesn't obey their stops. Put the order in the moment you're filled. If it gaps through, the gap rule takes over from there.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. Put it with the broker.
questions.simple: False. A stop in your head turns into a debate when price is diving, so put it with the broker.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41)

questions.q: A stock has all five boxes on its climax day. What else on your screen makes this the best version of the trade?
choices: The index is capitulating too
The market's calm and drifting up
It's day one of a market breakdown
It's falling alone on its own news
questions.why: The index capitulating too. When the whole market panics, people sell everything, good and bad, just to get out. That forced selling is what snaps back hardest. Look for the index stretched far under its 50-day, gapping down hard, better still on a Monday. Bracco also watches for a fast VIX move into 30. One stock falling alone has a story behind it, and the story doesn't go away overnight. And when the index is the one capitulating, the index fund itself is a trade.
questions.lesson_line: One stock crashing is a story. The whole market crashing is a setup.

wrong.The market's calm and drifting up: No panic in the market means nothing to snap back from.
wrong.It's day one of a market breakdown: Day one is the start of the fall. The first days of a crash are the worst time for this.
wrong.It's falling alone on its own news: A lone stock has a reason to fall. A whole market panicking is the better setup.

questions.simple: The whole market panicking too. Forced selling of everything is what snaps back hardest.

deeper.counter: Kell says the same from his side: get aggressive trading individual stocks when the index itself prints a Reversal Extension.

reasons: card line plus Kell and Bracco; proposed card context

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The trade is done when price reaches the daily ___ EMA from below.
questions.why: The 9 EMA. Bracco's studies make the 9 EMA the magnet; our rulebook keeps it as the parabolic target.
questions.lesson_line: Nine. The daily 9 EMA from below is where this trade ends.

questions.q: It's Friday and it's turning. What's your plan?
questions.story: A liquid ETF on a Friday afternoon. It's 20.3% down in 7 sessions and 5.6 ATR under its 50-day. Today it gapped down 4.1% on 3.1x volume with four of the five boxes, and it's turned up.
choices: Wait, Monday may bring a flush
Buy the close, the turn is in
Buy half now, add on Monday
Short it into the Monday open
questions.answer: Wait, Monday may bring a flush
questions.why: Wait. A lot of crashes put in the real low on a Monday. Bracco calls it the Monday Effect: notable capitulations and turns have come on Mondays. People sit with their losses all weekend, then dump at the open. In our study, three of the four failed trades were Friday buys, all stopped the next session. This chart is KRE. Monday gapped lower, traded through the Friday stop, and only then printed the real low. If you like it Friday, write the plan and watch Monday's open.
questions.lesson_line: Friday's turn is often Monday's gap. Let the weekend decide.

wrong.Short it into the Monday open: Not our trade. A stretch this big is where we look for the turn, not for more downside.
wrong.Buy the close, the turn is in: We buy the trigger during the day, never the close. And a Friday turn hasn't proved anything yet.
wrong.Buy half now, add on Monday: Half still eats the Monday gap. And there's no starter piece. One price, one stop.

questions.simple: Wait for Monday. Big turns often come on a Monday, and three of our four failures were Friday buys.

deeper.example: KRE was bought on the Friday of the tariff crash at 49.26, stop 47.09. Monday gapped to 47.50, traded 47.06 and then printed the real climax. The Friday buy was a day early, and the stop paid for it.

reasons: +1 fixed before

questions.q: You've been stopped out of this stock twice this week. Thursday it prints a fresh trigger. You can still take a third try.
questions.why: True. On one stock we allow 3 tries a week and 6 a month. This is your third, on a fresh trigger, so it's in. It gets its own stop and its own size, like a brand-new trade. Just know it's your last one this week. If it stops you again, the stock's telling you something. Walk away and go find a better one. The limit is there for the day you get stubborn.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week, six a month. After that, the stock's telling you something.
questions.simple: True. A third try on a fresh trigger is still inside our limit for the week.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E56)

questions.q: The peak four sessions ago was 88.00 and today's low is 50.00. How far has it fallen, in percent?
questions.why: 43.2%. The peak minus the low, over the peak: (88.00 - 50.00) / 88.00 = 43.2%. Kullamagi's premise for the long is a parabolic short that fell 50-60% or more in a few days. That is his bar. Our own DB example fell only 19.7% in 9 sessions, with four boxes ticked.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the fall from the peak to the climax low. Percent, then structure.
questions.simple: Peak minus low, divided by the peak, gives 43.2 percent.

reasons: computed key
the fall cut-offs are a held decision (D-118)

wrong.76.0%: Divided by the low instead of the peak.
wrong.38.0%: Gave the drop in dollars as a percent.
wrong.56.8%: Gave the low as a share of the peak.

questions.q: You'd buy at 20.50 with the stop at 19.80. The 9 EMA sits at 21.70. How much room is that, in R?
questions.why: 1.7R. Your risk is 20.50 minus 19.80, which is 0.70 a share. The room to the 9 EMA is 21.70 minus 20.50, which is 1.20. Then 1.20 over 0.70 is 1.7R. That's thin. You're risking 0.70 to make 1.20 if everything goes right. And only about 4 in 10 of these even reach the 9 EMA. I'd want a lot more room than that. I'd pass and look for the next one.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the room to the 9 EMA before you buy.
questions.simple: 1.7R of room. Risking 0.70 to make 1.20 is thin, so I'd pass.

reasons: computed key
the 2R room is the card's proposal

wrong.2.7R: You measured from the stop up to the 9 EMA. The room starts at your entry.
wrong.1.2R: That's the room in dollars. Divide it by your risk.
wrong.0.6R: Flipped. Divide the room by the risk, not the risk by the room.

questions.q: It gapped right through your stop. Where's your stop now?
questions.story: You bought at 30.00 with the stop at 29.00. Next morning it opens at 28.70, under your stop. The first 30-minute bar's low is 28.50.
choices: 28.50, the first 30-minute low
Sell at the open, 28.70
No stop until it's back over 29.00
Out now, the gap is past 2R
questions.why: 28.50, the low of the first 30-minute bar. A gap through your stop is the one time the stop moves down. You can't sell at 29.00 anymore, it's gone. Dumping at the open sells right into the panic, which can be the worst print of the day. So the first 30 minutes decide, and that bar's low becomes your new stop. There's a ceiling: if those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you're out. Your risk was one point. At 28.50 you'd be down a point and a half, still inside the ceiling.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.Sell at the open, 28.70: The gap rule gives it 30 minutes. Selling the open dumps you into the panic.
wrong.No stop until it's back over 29.00: You always have a stop. The new one is the first 30-minute low.
wrong.Out now, the gap is past 2R: It isn't. Down a point and a half on a one-point risk is inside 2R.

questions.simple: 28.50. After a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low becomes the new stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)

questions.q: Your buddy says lower your average. Do you add?
questions.story: Your parabolic long is down 1.5% from the fill, still above the stop. A friend says to buy more here so the average improves.
choices: No, we don't add to a loser
Yes, a lower average helps
Yes, but just a small add
No, but widen the stop for room
questions.answer: No, we don't add to a loser
questions.why: No. We buy the full size at one price with one stop, and we never add to a loser. Bracco says it plainly: 'I never add when I am down.' The average sounds like math. But your stop decides what you lose, not your average. More shares on the same stop means more dollars gone if it hits. And if it doesn't hit, you didn't need the extra shares to be right.
questions.lesson_line: A lower average on a loser is a bigger loser.

wrong.Yes, a lower average helps: A better average on a losing trade is more risk, not a better trade.
wrong.Yes, but just a small add: Small is still adding. One price, one stop.
wrong.No, but widen the stop for room: Not adding is right, but a stop only moves up, never wider.

questions.simple: No. More shares on the same stop is just a bigger loss if it hits.

deeper.trap: The friend's pitch sounds like math: the average improves. But the stop, not the average, decides what you lose. More shares with the same stop means more dollars lost if the stop hits. A re-entry needs a new trigger, not a lower price.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)
rebalanced choices: the lone No against three Yes was a tell

questions.q: What do you do with a stop that wide?
choices: Pass, wait for a tighter trigger
Full size, the stop is the stop
Move the stop up to fit full size
Take it, a 2x fund gets more room
questions.answer: Pass, wait for a tighter trigger
questions.why: Pass, and wait for a tighter trigger. 89.56 down to 83.01 is 7.3%. We like stops 1-3% away, 3.5% is still good, and we'll go up to 5%. Past that, we mostly wait. With a stop that wide the bounce has to run 7.3% just to pay you 1R. That's a lot to ask of a snap back that lives for days. Don't fix it by pulling the stop up. Under the climax low is where it belongs. In fairness, this one worked: 6.67R at its best. Wide ones sometimes do. We still pass on most of them.
questions.lesson_line: Past 5%, wait for a tighter trigger. Never pull the stop up to make it fit.

wrong.Full size, the stop is the stop: The stop is honest, but it's past our 5% line. Full size on that stop means a big loss if it hits.
wrong.Move the stop up to fit full size: That puts the stop above the climax low, inside the noise. A normal wiggle takes you out.
wrong.Take it, a 2x fund gets more room: Levered funds get no extra rules. Same stop, same 5% line.

questions.simple: Pass. The stop is past our 5% line, and pulling it up just puts it inside the noise.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A13)
the 8% skip line is the card's proposal, a number that can change

questions.story: A 2x silver fund turns on its climax day at 89.56. The low of the day puts your stop at 83.01, 7.3% under the fill.

questions.q: Your parabolic long is up 2R. You can move the stop up to breakeven now.
questions.why: True. Our window for breakeven runs from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell. 2R is the early end, and on this setup the early end makes sense. A snap back can roll over as fast as it came. Once you're up 2R, you don't want a winner turning into a loser. It's still a judgment, not a must. Some trades you give more room and move it later in the window.
questions.lesson_line: Up 2R on a snap back, the stop can go to breakeven.
questions.simple: True. Breakeven anywhere from 2R to 5R is ours, and fast snap backs favor the early end.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, a window)
2R is the card's pick inside that window
fixed before: flagged by the cold check

questions.q: It looks cheap here. Do you start buying?
questions.story: The climax day gaps down 6% and is still sliding at 10:00. It's 45% off its peak with every box ticked. Every tick looks cheaper.
choices: No, not before the turn
No, the gap has to fill first
Yes, the gap is the buy signal
Yes, a starter now, more at VWAP
questions.why: Not before the turn. Every box ticked makes it a candidate, not a trade. At 10:00 it's still sliding, and a falling stock can always fall more. That's buying the knife. The buy is the first 5-minute bar that closes back over VWAP, after the low. You'll pay up from the low, and that's fine. You're paying for proof that the panic stopped. Don't be too early.
questions.lesson_line: Cheap is not a trigger. The reclaim is.

wrong.Yes, a starter now, more at VWAP: A starter before the turn is still a knife. No starter piece, one entry, at the reclaim.
wrong.No, the gap has to fill first: A gap fill isn't our trigger. By then you've missed most of the bounce.
wrong.Yes, the gap is the buy signal: The gap is box five, part of the setup. The signal is the reclaim after the low.

questions.simple: No. Cheap isn't a signal, so wait for the first 5-minute close back over VWAP.

deeper.trap: Cheap feels safe, so every tick lower looks like a better price. It isn't. Until a 5-minute bar closes back over VWAP, the low may not be in. A trade under the climax low is the stop, and a new low means the selling wasn't done.

reasons: +2 pl.trigger_vwap is keyed while D-003 is still pending

questions.q: Bracco studied the climax day's opening volume. How does it compare to the other days of the burst?
choices: The heaviest open of the whole run
The lightest, sellers are tired
About the same as the other days
Heavy only if the gap fills
questions.answer: The heaviest open of the whole run
questions.why: The heaviest open of the whole run. Bracco says the climax day almost always shows the highest opening volume of the entire run. That's the crowd that held through the whole fall giving up at once, right at the open. He wrote it about the short, and we read it mirrored for the long. When you see that flood in the first 5 or 15 minutes, you're likely watching the climax. It's a read that raises the grade, not a must.
questions.lesson_line: The climax opens with the loudest crowd of the whole move.

wrong.The lightest, sellers are tired: The climax is the panic, so the open is the loudest, not the quietest.
wrong.About the same as the other days: A climax that looks like any other day isn't a climax.
wrong.Heavy only if the gap fills: Bracco ties the heavy open to the climax day itself. The gap filling has nothing to do with it.

questions.simple: The heaviest open of the run. That's the crowd giving up all at once.

reasons: +3 the claim rests on Bracco's word for the short; no test of it on the long side

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: After the entry, a trade under the ___ low means the selling was not done.
questions.why: The climax low. A trade under the climax low is the stop, and a new low means the selling was not done. Your stop sits a few cents under that low. The Wyckoff school reads a lower test the same way: new lows or a long consolidation.
questions.lesson_line: A new low under the climax says the panic is not finished. The stop agrees.
questions.simple: If price trades under the climax low, the panic is not over. That break is your stop.

reasons: settled stop rule A4 and F62; Wyckoff agrees

questions.q: Looking back, was the stop the mistake?
questions.story: A Friday climax with every box ticked. Our backtest bought it at 28.50 with the stop at 27.67. Monday's low of 27.44 took the stop. On March 23 the stock traded 17.95.
choices: No, it capped an early call at 1R
Yes, the stop needed more room
Yes, the wrong boxes were ticked
No, but sell at the close next time
questions.answer: No, it capped an early call at 1R
questions.why: No. The stop did exactly what it's for. This was the first week of a crash from an all-time high, and nobody could know that on the day. The buy was early. The stop turned that into a 1R loss instead of a 37% one. Judge the stop by what you knew when you set it, not by what came after. And one more thing. This was a stock under its 200-day, so today it's a pass for us before the stop even comes up.
questions.lesson_line: The stop keeps a week-early call at 1R. That's what it's for.

wrong.Yes, the stop needed more room: A wider stop would've ridden it down toward 17.95. The stop only moves up.
wrong.Yes, the wrong boxes were ticked: Every box was there. The problem was where the day sat: the first week of a crash.
wrong.No, but sell at the close next time: The stop is a real order with the broker. Waiting for the close lets the gap set your loss.

questions.simple: No. The buy was early, and the stop kept it to 1R, which is its whole job.

deeper.trap: Don't judge the stop by what came after. The stock traded 17.95 on March 23, but nobody could see that on the day of the buy. The stop turns an unknowable early call into a known 1R loss.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's stop rule (A4, D41)

questions.q: Same climax, two names: both tick all five boxes. For one the index is capitulating too; for the other it is calm. Grade?
choices: The first; the market backs it
Equal; the five boxes decide
The second; a calm index is safer
The first; skip the second one
questions.answer: The first; the market backs it
questions.why: The first. The same five boxes grade higher when the index is capitulating too. A calm index, or one only starting to break down, weakens the case. Same boxes, different grade.
questions.lesson_line: Grade the market with the stock. A calm index drops the grade.

wrong.The second; a calm index is safer: A calm index means no market panic to snap back from. That weakens the case.
wrong.Equal; the five boxes decide: The boxes are the pattern. The market is the context, and context changes the grade.
wrong.The first; skip the second one: A calm index lowers the grade. Nothing in the card says it voids the trade.

questions.simple: The name with a panicking index grades higher. The market adds to the pattern, so the same boxes do not always grade the same.

reasons: +2 touches D-023 (market reading) through the new fourth choice
+1 fixed before

questions.q: It's setting up again. How do you treat it?
questions.story: Your parabolic long reached the 9 EMA on day two and the trade is done. Two weeks later the stock has built a tight range.
choices: A new trade with its own stop
The same trade, keep the old stop
Skip it, the bounce is spent
Buy the break with a wider stop
questions.answer: A new trade with its own stop
questions.why: A new trade with its own stop. The parabolic trade ended at the 9 EMA. That was the plan, and it's done. A tight range two weeks later is a different setup. It gets its own entry, its own stop under its own low, and its own size. Bracco sees two paths after a crash: a fast bounce, or a tight range for a few weeks. If you get the range, it goes on your radar like any other setup, with every normal rule, the 200-day included.
questions.lesson_line: The bounce is one trade. The range after it is another.

wrong.The same trade, keep the old stop: That trade ended at the 9 EMA. Anything after it starts fresh.
wrong.Skip it, the bounce is spent: The first trade is spent, but a tight range can be a new setup.
wrong.Buy the break with a wider stop: A new trade gets an honest stop under its own low, not a wider one.

questions.simple: A new trade. The parabolic one ended at the 9 EMA, so the range gets its own entry and stop.

reasons: +1 rests on the card's hold-longer line (c21); the exit fraction (D-013) is held but the key no longer leans on it

questions.q: Your parabolic long gaps up at the open, right past where you planned to sell some. You have to sell at the open.
questions.why: False. A gap past your sell level isn't an automatic sell. Selling some into a big gap is your call. Sometimes the gap is the move and taking some off is smart. Sometimes it keeps running and you're glad you held. That's judgment, never a rule. A gap down through your stop is a different story. That one follows the gap rule.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past your sell level is a choice, not an order.
questions.simple: False. Selling into a gap at the open is a judgment call, never a rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)

questions.q: The pattern's perfect. Can you take it?
questions.story: A $7 stock is down 55% in three days with all five boxes and a VWAP reclaim. It trades about $6 million a day.
choices: No, under $10 and $20M a day
No, the burst is too fast to trust
Yes, at half size for the spread
Yes, small caps are where it happens
questions.why: No. We only trade stocks at $10 or more that do at least $20 million a day. This one's $7 and does about $6 million. A perfect pattern doesn't fix that. In a panic a thin stock is exactly where you get trapped. The spread blows out, your stop fills way under where you put it, and there's nobody to sell to. Bracco says this setup shows up more in small caps, and he still prefers mid to large caps.
questions.lesson_line: A textbook burst in a thin stock is still a thin stock.

wrong.No, the burst is too fast to trust: Speed is the setup. It fails on price and dollar volume.
wrong.Yes, at half size for the spread: Half size doesn't make a thin stock liquid. The rule is about the stock.
wrong.Yes, small caps are where it happens: Common isn't tradable. We need $10 and $20 million a day.

questions.simple: No. It's under $10 and under $20 million a day, and thin stocks trap you in a panic.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's B23 rule; D-018 is held but both options keep this key

questions.q: Bracco says this setup shows up more often in small caps. What does he prefer to trade it in?
choices: Mid and large caps
Small caps, where it's most common
Any cheap stock that gapped down
Thin names that move the fastest
questions.why: Mid and large caps. Small caps crash like this more often, but they're thin and they gap through stops. Bigger names have the liquidity to get in and out when everyone's panicking. Then check the 200-day. After a crash this hard a lot of names sit under it, and down there we don't buy stocks at all. So the trade often goes to the index fund or a levered ETF.
questions.lesson_line: Pick the name too. Liquid, mid and large caps first.

wrong.Any cheap stock that gapped down: Cheap is a warning. We need $10 and $20 million a day at least.
wrong.Small caps, where it's most common: Common doesn't mean tradable. Bracco prefers mid to large caps.
wrong.Thin names that move the fastest: Fast and thin is how a stop fills way under your price.

questions.simple: Mid and large caps. They're liquid enough to get in and out in a panic.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23, D42, E54)

questions.q: What's the read on the setting?
questions.story: A China-based stock. Six names from the same hot group print this climax on the same day. This one gapped down 4.5% on 7.2x volume with all five boxes.
choices: A group unwind, the best setting
Pass, many names at once is a crash
Neutral, the group changes nothing
Wait a week for a retest
questions.answer: A group unwind, the best setting
questions.why: A group unwind, the best setting. When a crowded group dumps all at once, it's forced selling: funds and traders all heading for the same door. Once they're out, the selling dries up fast and the whole group can snap back together. HTHT was one of six that day, and 3R came the next session. Check the whole market too. A group unwind is great, but the first week of a market-wide crash is the worst setting. And HTHT was a stock under its 200-day, so today we'd play this through an index fund or a levered ETF.
questions.lesson_line: When a whole crowd gets out at once, the turn is a group event.

wrong.Pass, many names at once is a crash: One theme unwinding is the best setting. A market-wide crash is the worst, so check the index.
wrong.Neutral, the group changes nothing: A whole group flushing at once is what makes this setup strongest.
wrong.Wait a week for a retest: The buy is the reclaim on the climax day. A week later is a different trade.

questions.simple: A whole group flushing at once is forced selling, and that's the best setting for this trade.

deeper.example: HTHT, July 2021, the China liquidation: six names fired on 2021-07-27. It was 29.0% off the high in 16 sessions, with a 4.5% gap down on 7.2x volume. Buy 40.75, stop 38.97, and 3R came the next session.

reasons: +1 fixed before

questions.q: Your parabolic long is up 2R and the company reports tomorrow. You can hold it through the report.
questions.why: False. We only hold through a report when the trade's up 5R. At 2R you sell before it. A report can gap the stock right through your stop, and no stop order catches a gap. At 5R the gain is big enough to absorb a bad one. At 2R, one ugly gap wipes out the win and then some.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings is a gap you can't stop. 5R buys the ticket. 2R doesn't.
questions.simple: False. We hold through a report only at 5R or more, and 2R isn't there.

deeper.example: GE's parabolic long reached 3R the session after its report gapped it up, so that hold carried earnings risk. A gap up pays. A gap down goes through the stop, and the gap rule then decides your exit.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's B22 rule

questions.q: Your account is 40,000 and you risk 0.5%. Fill 76.76, stop 73.20. How many shares do you buy?
questions.why: 56 shares. Start with the risk: 0.5% of 40,000 is $200. Then the risk per share: 76.76 minus 73.20 is 3.56. 200 over 3.56 is 56.2, so you round down to 56. Never round up, or you're over your risk. That stop is 4.6% away, wider than we like but inside our 5%. So the answer is fewer shares, never a tighter stop. One more thing: this chart is BABA, a stock far under its 200-day. Today we'd only run this on an index or a levered ETF. The math is the same.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. Never the other way round.
questions.simple: Risk dollars over the gap from fill to stop, rounded down, is 56 shares.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A5)

choices: 57 shares
521 shares
561 shares
56 shares

wrong.57 shares: Rounded up. That puts you over your 0.5% risk.
wrong.521 shares: That's the whole account divided by the price. The size comes from the stop.
wrong.561 shares: Moved the decimal on 0.5%. That's ten times the risk.

questions.story: A climax-day turn from our study of past crashes, worked as a sizing drill.

questions.q: Down 20% in three weeks. Does it go on your parabolic long list?
questions.story: Over three weeks a stock drifts from 60 to 48 in small, overlapping bars: a down day or two, then a bounce. Volume stays flat. Today it closes at the low.
choices: No, it's an orderly decline
Yes, it's already 20% down
Yes, if tomorrow gaps down hard
No, it's not an RS leader
questions.why: No. It's an orderly decline, a grind. Small overlapping bars, a bounce every few days, flat volume. Nobody's panicking. The selling is steady, and steady selling can go on for months. Our setup needs the fall to speed up: steeper legs, gap downs, volume climbing into a climax. Bracco calls judging by percent alone, ignoring the structure, a frequent mistake. Twenty percent down slowly is a grind, not a burst.
questions.lesson_line: Twenty percent down slowly is a grind. The setup needs a burst.

wrong.Yes, if tomorrow gaps down hard: One gap on a slow grind isn't a burst. The steeper days and rising volume are still missing.
wrong.Yes, it's already 20% down: Percent alone is the mistake. The shape here is a slow, overlapping drift.
wrong.No, it's not an RS leader: Parabolic trades skip the RS rule. The shape is what fails here.

questions.simple: No. The bars overlap and volume is flat, so it's steady selling, not a panic to snap back from.

reasons: +1 fixed before

questions.q: The bounce came anyway, just a week late. What's the lesson?
questions.story: Our backtest bought a Friday turn at 25.58, stop 24.94. Monday closed 24.49, through the stop. The low came Thursday at 23.85. By Friday the stock was back at the 9 EMA.
choices: Take the stop, the selling wasn't done
Hold, it got to the 9 EMA anyway
Widen the stop to the Monday low
Add Monday to lower your cost
questions.answer: Take the stop, the selling wasn't done
questions.why: Take the stop. Monday closed 24.49, through your 24.94 stop, and a new low means the selling wasn't done. Yes, it got back to the 9 EMA by Friday. But it got there from 23.85, a lower low, and on Monday you couldn't know where the low would be. Hold through a stop on the ones that come back and you'll hold through the ones that don't. The trade that worked came later, on a fresh turn, as a new trade with its own stop. And notice it was a Friday buy again. Three of our four failures were. One more thing: WDC was a stock under its 200-day, so today it's a pass for us anyway.
questions.lesson_line: The first turn is often a day early. The stop costs 1R, and the next turn is a new trade.

wrong.Add Monday to lower your cost: Never add to a loser. A re-entry needs a new trigger, as a new trade.
wrong.Hold, it got to the 9 EMA anyway: It got there from a lower low. You can't hold through stops on the ones that happen to come back.
wrong.Widen the stop to the Monday low: The stop only moves up. Moving it down is how a 1R loss grows.

questions.simple: Take the stop. A close through it means the selling isn't done, even if a bounce comes later.

deeper.trap: The hard part is that the first turn looked right: a gap-down day, bought on the reclaim, on a Friday. Three of the four failed examples in our study were Friday buys, with the real low on the Monday or later. Don't buy the Friday before a possible Monday flush.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)
worked example from our own bars, not yet reviewed by the owner
fixed before: the key was the only choice phrased as an observation

questions.q: When the index itself is capitulating, a 3x index ETF is a fine way to play the turn, with no extra rules.
questions.why: True. We like the levered ETFs, and they get no extra rules. Same trigger, same stop a few cents under the low, same size math. Along with the index itself, they're the only way we buy under the 200-day. When the whole market washes out, a 3x fund gives you the snap back with real punch. It also swings three times as hard, so its stop sits further away in percent. The size math takes care of that. Your share count comes down and your risk stays the same.
questions.lesson_line: For the index turn, the 3x fund is a tool, not an exception.
questions.simple: True. Levered ETFs are preferred for the index turn, with no special rules.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E54)

questions.q: The name you're buying trades 500,000 shares a day on average. What's the most shares you can own?
choices: 5,000 shares
10,000 shares
2,500 shares
50,000 shares
questions.why: 5,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 500,000 is 5,000. On this setup it matters more than anywhere. You're buying in a panic, and if it fails you need out in a hurry. Own too big a piece of the daily volume and your own selling moves the price against you. This cap sits on top of your risk-based size. You take whichever is smaller.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume. In a panic, getting out is the whole game.

wrong.10,000 shares: That's double our cap. The limit is 1% of the daily volume, 5,000 shares.
wrong.2,500 shares: That's half the cap. One percent of 500,000 is 5,000.
wrong.50,000 shares: That's ten times our limit. You'd never get out clean.

questions.simple: 1% of 500,000 shares is 5,000. Own more and your own selling moves the price.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)
its 3x ETF liquidity exception is a held decision (D-018)

questions.q: It gapped through your stop. What do you do after the first 30 minutes?
questions.story: You bought at 52.00 with the stop at 50.90. Next morning it opens at 49.50. The first 30-minute bar's low is 48.70.
choices: Out, a 3R loss is past 2R
48.70 is the new stop, hold on
Hold and wait for the close
Sell half now, hold the rest
questions.why: You're out. Your risk was 52.00 minus 50.90, which is 1.10 a share. The first 30-minute low is 48.70, and 52.00 minus 48.70 is 3.30. Then 3.30 over 1.10 is 3R. The gap rule lets those 30 minutes set a new stop, but only while the loss stays inside 2R. This one's way past it. Get out and take the hit. A gap that big is the market telling you the trade broke overnight.
questions.lesson_line: The gap rule has a ceiling. Past 2R in the first 30 minutes, you're done.

wrong.Hold and wait for the close: The first 30 minutes decide, not the close.
wrong.48.70 is the new stop, hold on: The 30-minute low only becomes the stop while the loss stays inside 2R. This is 3R.
wrong.Sell half now, hold the rest: The rule has two outcomes: a new stop, or out past 2R. Half is neither.

questions.simple: Out. The first 30 minutes took the loss past 2R, so the gap rule says leave.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's gap rule (B20)
+2 the key needs arithmetic: 48.70 is a 3R loss

questions.q: One kind of parabolic long is a blow-off unwinding. What did the chart do before the crash?
choices: A fast run up, a blow-off top
A quiet base near the highs
A slow downtrend for months
An earnings gap, then a fade
questions.answer: A fast run up, a blow-off top
questions.why: A fast run up, a blow-off top. The stock went vertical first, set up as a parabolic short, then cracked. Bracco has seen blown-off shorts turn into parabolic longs in just a couple of days. Everyone who chased the top is now trapped and selling. Once they're flushed out, the stretch snaps back. No run, no rubber band.
questions.lesson_line: The unwind needs a blow-off before it. No run, no rubber band.

wrong.An earnings gap, then a fade: One gap and a fade isn't a blow-off. The unwind needs a vertical run first.
wrong.A quiet base near the highs: A base is a rest, not a run. The unwind follows a stock that went vertical.
wrong.A slow downtrend for months: That's the other kind, a capitulation at the end of a long decline. The unwind starts from a run up.

questions.simple: A fast vertical run up. The crash flushes out everyone who chased the top.

reasons: +3 the 50% run rests on one card line (c29)
+2 a proposed threshold that can change

questions.q: Which trade is setting up here?
questions.story: A stock has three straight up days and two gap-up opens, each day a bigger gain than the last. Today it gaps up again, then breaks under VWAP by 10:30.
choices: A parabolic short, the burst ran up
A parabolic long, it's the climax gap
A U&R long off intraday VWAP
Neither, a burst needs five days
questions.answer: A parabolic short, the burst ran up
questions.why: A parabolic short. The burst ran up: three up days, two gap ups, bigger gains each day, and today's climax gaps up. Breaking under VWAP is the short's trigger, with the stop over the day's high. Our long is the same five boxes upside down: a burst down and a gap down. So the first thing you check is which way the climax gapped. Up is the short. Down is the long.
questions.lesson_line: Check which way it gapped. Up is the short, down is the long.

wrong.A parabolic long, it's the climax gap: Our long's climax gaps down. This one gapped up after three up days.
wrong.A U&R long off intraday VWAP: A U&R undercuts a visible low after a dip. Three vertical up days into a gap is a burst.
wrong.Neither, a burst needs five days: The burst is 3 to 5 days, and the climax gap comes on day 3 to 5. These days fit.

questions.simple: A parabolic short. It ran up and gapped up, and the long is the same picture pointing down.

deeper.trap: The long and the short share the same five boxes, so only the direction tells them apart. Check which way the climax gap points before you pick a side. Up is the short, entered as it breaks under VWAP with the stop over the high. Down is the long, entered on a reclaim of VWAP with the stop under the low.

reasons: +2 pl.climax_gap is held (D-119); the gap is taught as a tell, not a gate

questions.q: One heavy afternoon, then a turn. Which setup is this?
questions.story: A leader fresh out of a base drops 2 ATR in one afternoon into its old high. No low is undercut. The volume is the day's heaviest, then it turns. Yesterday it closed at a high.
choices: Mean Reversion, a one-day flush
A parabolic long, it fell 2 ATR
A U&R off the old high
A dead-cat bounce, a one-day fall
questions.why: Mean Reversion. One sharp afternoon flush in a leader, into a level, is that setup. A parabolic long needs the whole burst behind it: 3 to 5 straight down days, two gap downs, rising volume. So count the down days first. Here there's one. A leader that dips hard for a few hours is a different animal from a stock that's panicked for a week. You trade it differently.
questions.lesson_line: Count the down days. One day in a leader is Mean Reversion. Three to five is parabolic.

wrong.A parabolic long, it fell 2 ATR: One afternoon isn't a burst. The burst is 3 to 5 straight down days with two gap downs.
wrong.A U&R off the old high: A U&R needs an undercut of a visible low. Nothing was undercut here.
wrong.A dead-cat bounce, a one-day fall: A dead-cat bounce starts with a big one-day gap down on news. This one's an afternoon flush in a leader.

questions.simple: Mean Reversion. It's one afternoon, and a parabolic long needs 3 to 5 straight down days.

deeper.trap: Count the days before you name the setup. One heavy afternoon in a leader fits Mean Reversion, even with big volume and a quick turn. A parabolic long needs the whole burst behind it: 3 to 5 straight down days, two gap downs and rising volume. Heavy volume alone names neither.

reasons: card lookalike row; Mean Reversion is taught in another unit

questions.q: Which setup family does this trade belong to?
questions.story: A 2x-3x ETF is 20% under its 200-day after a four-day, 60% fall with two gap downs. The index is capitulating too. After the low, the ETF reclaims VWAP.
choices: Parabolic, a U&R needs a level
A U&R, VWAP is the level
A flat base, wait for the pivot
None, it's under the 200-day
questions.answer: Parabolic, a U&R needs a level
questions.why: Parabolic. A U&R undercuts a visible low that everyone's watching, in a name above its 200-day. This has no level. It's a four-day, 60% crash with two gap downs and the index capitulating with it. That's a burst, and the VWAP reclaim after the low is the parabolic trigger. It can be bought under the 200-day because it's a levered ETF. A stock in this same spot would be a no.
questions.lesson_line: No level, under the 200-day, a levered ETF after a crash: that's parabolic, not a U&R.

wrong.A U&R, VWAP is the level: VWAP is the trigger, not a level. A U&R needs a visible low and a name above its 200-day.
wrong.A flat base, wait for the pivot: Nothing is basing. A four-day crash is a burst.
wrong.None, it's under the 200-day: That's the rule for stocks. Indexes and levered ETFs are the exception on a parabolic long.

questions.simple: Parabolic. There's no level being undercut, and a levered ETF can be bought under its 200-day.

deeper.trap: Under the 200-day, stocks are a hard no. The exception is an index or a levered ETF on a parabolic long. Don't stretch it to a U&R. A U&R needs a visible low and a name above its 200-day. A parabolic long needs no level.

reasons: +2 D-009 (the 200-day exception) is held; only B26's own exception is keyed

questions.q: This chart ends on the gap-down climax day. Go box by box. How many of the five does it tick?
choices: Five of five
Four of five
Three of five
Two of five
questions.why: All five. Three straight lower closes, two gap downs in a row, losses getting bigger, volume rising, and today's gap down. It fell 25.6% in 8 sessions, gapped down 2.2% on 3.5x volume and closed 2.8% above its open. Now the honest part. The boxes read the fall, not the market, so they can't tell you if the selling's done. And this is GE, a stock under its 200-day. As a stock it's a pass for us, however many boxes it ticks.
questions.lesson_line: Five boxes and a strong close on the gap-down day. That's the picture.

wrong.Four of five: Go box by box: closes, gaps, bigger losses, rising volume, the climax gap. They're all there.
wrong.Three of five: You missed two. Count the gap downs and the rising volume again.
wrong.Two of five: All five are on this chart. Start with the three lower closes and work through.

questions.simple: All five boxes show. Boxes read the fall, but not whether the selling is done.

deeper.trap: Five boxes aren't a guarantee. At the start of one crash, 83 names printed a gap-down reversal on heavy volume with every box ticked. None reached 5R. It was the first week of a breakdown. The boxes read the fall, and the market has to say whether the selling is done.

reasons: a worked example read from our own bars
the box count is a held decision (D-002)
fixed before: the old key had no balanced second 'Take it' choice

questions.q: This chart ends on a crash-day gap down. The stock ran 1.5x its average volume while SPY ran 4.1x. What's that telling you?
choices: The panic's in the index, not here
A full climax, so take the VWAP reclaim
Sellers are done, buy the gap
Nothing, volume never matters
questions.answer: The panic's in the index, not here
questions.why: The panic's in the index, not in this stock. On a real climax the crowd is dumping this name: heavy volume, the heaviest open of the run. Here SPY traded 4.1 times its average and this stock only 1.5 times. It got dragged down with the market without its own holders giving up. Light volume doesn't kill a setup, but it lowers the grade. Here it didn't matter anyway. APD was a stock under its 200-day, so it's a pass for us. It was stopped the next day at 243.69.
questions.lesson_line: The crowd has to be in this stock, not just in the index.

wrong.A full climax, so take the VWAP reclaim: Its own volume never showed up. And a stock under its 200-day is a pass for us.
wrong.Sellers are done, buy the gap: Buying the gap is buying before the turn. And light volume says its sellers never had their flush.
wrong.Nothing, volume never matters: Volume doesn't make or break it, but it raises or lowers the grade. Here it says the crowd wasn't in this one.

questions.simple: The panic was in the index. This stock's own holders never had their flush, so it's a weak setup.

deeper.example: APD on the tariff-crash Monday, 2025-04-07. It had four of five boxes and a 1.7% gap. Its volume was 1.5x its average, while SPY ran 4.1x. Taken anyway, it was stopped the next day at 243.69.

reasons: +2 the 2x line is a card proposal and can change

questions.q: In Bracco's studies, a lot of the notable capitulations and turns came on a Monday.
questions.why: True. He calls it the Monday Effect: through his studies, notable capitulations and turns have come on Mondays. It makes sense. People sit with their losses all weekend, then dump at Monday's open, and that last wave of selling can be the low. It's his observation, not a law. It's also why we're careful buying a Friday turn. Three of our four failed trades were Friday buys.
questions.lesson_line: Big turns love a Monday. Be careful buying the Friday before one.
questions.simple: True. He calls it the Monday Effect, and it's an observation, not a rule.

deeper.trap: Do not turn this into a rule that every Monday is a buy. It is Bracco's observation that notable turns have come on Mondays. It is also why we do not buy the Friday before one: three of our four failures were Friday buys.

reasons: +3 the Monday effect rests on Bracco's own studies, one cited source

questions.q: How wide is that stop, in percent of your fill?
questions.why: 7.17%. 20.50 minus 19.03 is 1.47, and 1.47 over 20.50 is 7.17%. That's past our 5% line, so I'd pass here, or wait for a tighter trigger. We like 1-3%, and up to 5% is fine. Don't fix it by nudging the stop up. Under the climax low is where it belongs, because a new low means the selling wasn't done. This one did reach 3R in 6 sessions. Wide ones sometimes work. We still pass on most. And this was SLG, a stock under its 200-day, so it's a pass twice over.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop before the size. Past 5%, wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.simple: The stop sits 7.17% under the fill. That's past our 5% line, so you pass or wait for a tighter one.

deeper.trap: Don't nudge the stop up to make the percent look smaller. The stop sits a few cents under the climax low because a new low means the selling wasn't done. A tighter stop only hides the real distance, and the size math then makes you too big for the risk.

reasons: computed key
the 8% skip line is the card's proposal, a number that can change

wrong.7.72%: You divided by the stop. Measure the distance as a share of your fill.
wrong.1.47%: That's the gap in dollars, 1.47. Divide it by the fill.
wrong.92.83%: That's the stop as a share of the fill, not the distance down to it.

questions.story: The turn on a climax day fills at 20.50. The low of the day puts your stop at 19.03.

questions.q: It's gone nowhere for two weeks. What do you do with it?
questions.story: Ten trading days after the climax, your parabolic long sits at 0.6R. The stop was never touched, and the 9 EMA is still above.
choices: Sell it, under 1R after 10 days
Hold, the stop was never hit
Add, it proved the low is in
Raise the stop, give it a month
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days gets sold, even if the stop never got touched. It's a snap-back trade. It's supposed to work in days. Bracco says these aren't meant to be held longer than 1-3 days. Ten days at 0.6R means the snap back didn't come, and that money can go to a fresh setup that's actually moving.
questions.lesson_line: This bounce lives for days. Ten days under 1R and the money has a better home.

wrong.Hold, the stop was never hit: The stop is one exit. Time is the other.
wrong.Add, it proved the low is in: Not to a trade going nowhere. A bounce that stalls proves nothing.
wrong.Raise the stop, give it a month: A month is way past our 10 days. Sell it and move on.

questions.simple: Sell it. A snap back should work in days, and ten days under 1R means it didn't.

deeper.trap: The stop isn't the only exit. Time is another. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is tying up money a fresh setup could use.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's C33 rule; D-019 may shorten the time stop, and this key holds under both options

questions.q: When we tested it, most parabolic longs reached the 9 EMA before the climax low broke.
questions.why: False. Only about 4 in 10 got to the 9 EMA before the day's low broke. Bracco's studies show the 9 EMA acting as a magnet on his shorts. On longs, our test says it's not that reliable. So the 9 EMA is still the target, but it's a target, not a promise. That's why the stop matters so much on this trade, and why you don't hold and hope.
questions.lesson_line: The 9 EMA is the target, not a promise.
questions.simple: False. Only about 4 in 10 reached the 9 EMA first, so it's a target, not a promise.

deeper.counter: Bracco's claim is from his studies of the short: the 9-day EMA acts as a magnet for mean reversion. Our daily test of longs found only about 4 in 10 got there before the day's low broke. After a crash from far above, the 9 EMA can be out of reach, as with CAR and AGQ.

reasons: +3 the 4 in 10 comes from one card line (c19)
+2 a number from our own test that can change

questions.q: How do you think about the target on this one?
choices: Don't count on the 9 EMA soon
The 9 EMA is days away at most
Expect a bounce as big as the fall
Widen the stop to give it time
questions.answer: Don't count on the 9 EMA soon
questions.why: Don't count on the 9 EMA soon. After a crash that fast, the 9 EMA is still way up near the old prices. Here it was above 260 at the end of April, with price near 202.31. Getting there isn't a bounce, it's a big recovery, and it took until 05-21. When the target's that far off, don't expect it in days, and don't widen your stop to wait for it. Room to the target is good. A target in another zip code is a warning.
questions.lesson_line: Room to the target is good. A target in another zip code is a warning.

wrong.The 9 EMA is days away at most: Not after a crash this fast. It took until 05-21 here.
wrong.Expect a bounce as big as the fall: Nothing promises that. A bigger crash just puts the target further away.
wrong.Widen the stop to give it time: The stop only moves up, never wider.

questions.simple: After a crash this fast, the 9 EMA can be weeks away, so don't count on it soon.

deeper.counter: Bracco's magnet claim for the 9 EMA is for his short. For longs it doesn't hold up as well. CAR fell from 847.70 to 202.31 in three sessions. Its 9 EMA, above 260 at the end of April, wasn't reached until 05-21.

reasons: a worked example read from our own bars
a date that changes with the data
the quote sits in the criteria card, not the research note the source cites

questions.story: A three-session crash from 847.70 to 202.31. The 9 EMA is still way up above the price, and today it turns.

questions.q: Perfect bars everywhere. What actually decides this one?
questions.story: An index fund. It's one of 83 names that print the climax on the same Friday: every box ticked, every context met, heavy volume. It's the start of a market slide from an all-time high.
choices: What the whole market is doing
The box count, five beats four
The volume, heaviest day wins
The RS rating, leaders hold up
questions.answer: What the whole market is doing
questions.why: What the whole market is doing. On that Friday, 83 names printed this climax with every box ticked, every context met and heavy volume. Not one reached 5R. All were stopped. It was the first week of a breakdown from an all-time high, and the real low came 16 sessions later. The bars can't see that. Only the bigger picture can. Check our market reading in the app and the index's trend. Ask whether we're at the start of a fall or the end of one. The first days of a crash are the worst time for this trade.
questions.lesson_line: Perfect bars in the first week of a crash are still the first week of a crash.

wrong.The box count, five beats four: Every one of the 83 had every box. The count couldn't separate them.
wrong.The volume, heaviest day wins: Volume was heavy across the board. It couldn't tell the failures from a real turn.
wrong.The RS rating, leaders hold up: Parabolic trades skip the RS rule, and all 83 were stopped, leaders or not.

questions.simple: The state of the whole market. Perfect bars in the first week of a crash failed all 83 times.

deeper.example: On 2020-02-28, 83 names printed a gap-down reversal on heavy volume with every box and context ticked. Not one reached 5R and all were stopped. BAC was one: bought 28.50, stopped at 27.67, and it traded 17.95 on 03-23.

reasons: +2 the 83 and 16 come from one dated read of our own data

questions.q: What went wrong on this one?
questions.story: A regional bank in the 2023 panic. Our backtest bought its turn at 23.10, stop 21.70. Day one closed at 21.27, down 7.9%, stopped out. Six sessions later another bank turned and ran.
choices: The buy came one leg too early
Never buy a bank in a panic
Next time, use a wider stop
The setup was fake from the start
questions.answer: The buy came one leg too early
questions.why: One leg too early. The setup fit, but the panic had one more leg in it, down to 19.04. Six sessions later the real turn came in another bank. That's the cost of reading a climax off the bars: sometimes you're early. The stop kept it to one loss. Two more things would keep you out of this one today. That stop was 6.1% away, past our 5% line. And BKU was a stock under its 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A turn in a panic can come one leg early. Let the stop pay for it.

wrong.Never buy a bank in a panic: The sector wasn't the problem. The timing inside the panic was.
wrong.Next time, use a wider stop: A wider stop pays more for the same early call. The stop only moves up.
wrong.The setup was fake from the start: The setup fit. The panic just had one more leg.

questions.simple: It was one leg early. The panic had more to go, and the stop kept the damage to one loss.

deeper.trap: Being early is the price of reading a climax off the bars. BKU fit the setup and was stopped on day one: it closed down 7.9%, and the panic ran to 19.04. SLG turned six sessions later. The stop under the climax low keeps the cost of being early to one loss.

reasons: +1 fixed before

questions.q: Do you take the second try?
questions.story: You were stopped out of a parabolic long on Tuesday. Thursday the same stock prints a new low, turns and reclaims VWAP again, with every box and rule still met. It would be your second try this week.
choices: Yes, a new trade with its own stop
No, a stop-out ends that setup
Yes, but with a wider stop
No, wait for it to hit the 9 EMA
questions.answer: Yes, a new trade with its own stop
questions.why: Yes, as a brand-new trade. After a stop-out we buy again only if the setup triggers again. It just did: a new low, a turn, a VWAP reclaim. So it gets its own stop a few cents under the new low, its own size, every rule. It's your second try this week, inside our limit of 3 a week and 6 a month. Just be honest with yourself. A fresh trigger is a reason. Wanting your money back isn't.
